ex01: ReferenceError: a name that doesn't exist. TypeError: an operation on the wrong kind of value. RangeError: a number outside the allowed range. SyntaxError: code JavaScript can't even read.
Reassigning a const is an operation that isn't allowed on that variable.
A variable name can't start with a digit, so JavaScript can't parse that line at all.
ex02: Check for the problem before doing the subtraction.
Withdrawing exactly the whole balance is fine. Only more than the balance is a problem.
After a throw, the function stops: no need for an else.
ex03: typeof tells you whether a value is a number.
Throw when the type is NOT 'number'. Strings with digits, like '3', are not numbers.
Use the TypeError constructor, not the plain Error one.
ex04: There are two ways to be out of range: too low or too high. One condition with || can catch both.
Return the label with a template literal after the check.
ex05: Write one `if` per rule, in the order listed, each one throwing right away.
Once all the checks have passed, the last line can calculate and return the price.
A 20% discount on 100 removes 20: the price times the percent, divided by 100.
ex06: Put the risky call, JSON.parse, inside the try block and return its result from there.
The catch block runs only when JSON.parse throws. What should the function return in that case?
ex07: Call fn inside a try block.
In the catch block, the error object has a property with its text.
If the try block finishes without errors, the function continues after the try/catch.
ex08: Like the previous exercise, but now you need two properties of the error.
Join the name and the message with a colon and a space.
ex09: Wrap the call to action in a try block, with a finally block after it. You don't need catch.
A return inside try still runs the finally block before the function ends.
Unlocking belongs in finally, so it happens whether the action works or throws.
ex10: Number('') is 0, so check for empty text yourself before trusting the conversion. trim() removes the spaces.
Number.isNaN tells you whether the conversion failed.
Check the type problems first, then the negative numbers.
ex11: The return inside try only happens when divide doesn't throw.
In catch, build the failure object using the error's message.
Both results are objects with an `ok` property. Only the property next to it changes.
ex12: Inside the catch, check what kind of error you got before deciding what to do.
Invalid JSON produces a SyntaxError. instanceof can check that.
Once other errors are thrown again, run the tests: the error that shows up points to the hidden bug.
ex13: A string can be thrown, but it isn't an Error object.
Create an Error with the same message and throw that instead.
ex14: Follow the NotFoundError example in the comment, changing the names.
The class needs `export` before it so the tests can see it.
Strings have a method that tells you whether they contain another string.
ex15: Call fn inside try. If it doesn't throw, return 'ok' right after it.
In catch, use instanceof to check whether the error is a ValidationError.
For any other error, throw the same error object again.
ex16: Write one guard clause per rule, in the order listed.
A name made only of spaces is empty after trim().
Number.isInteger returns false for strings, decimals and undefined, which covers every bad age.
ex17: After a throw, the rest of the try block is skipped and the catch block runs.
finally runs in both cases: with or without an error.
After the catch handles the error, the code after the try/catch keeps running normally.
ex18: Use a loop that runs `times` times, with a try/catch inside it.
Returning from inside the try ends the loop and the function as soon as a call works.
Keep the last error in a variable declared before the loop, and throw it after the loop.
ex19: Start with an empty array and push a message for each problem you find. Don't return early.
A missing or empty username is falsy. The length check only makes sense when there is a username.
To find a digit, go through the characters of the password and check whether one of them is in '0123456789'.
ex20: Split the text on ';', trim each entry, and skip the empty ones.
Find the position of the first '='. The key is everything before it and the value everything after it.
Before adding a key, check whether it is already in the object. Module 07 showed two ways to do that.
